name: Gore-Tex lip implant (SoftForm)
lead: Gore-Tex lip implants are strips or tubes of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) that a surgeon places in the lip to add permanent volume and definition, an option for people who want fuller lips from a solid implant instead of repeated injectable fillers. Wikipedia describes them as 1.6 mm or 4.8 mm in diameter and names Advanta, UltraSoft and SoftForm as commercial versions.[1]

ePTFE is also used as a graft and implant material in vascular, cardiac, hernia and facial plastic surgery.[2] SoftForm was developed for facial soft-tissue augmentation, and a 2000 historical review described it as a subcutaneous implant created for deep nasolabial folds and other facial furrows.[3] Advanta, made by Atrium Medical, is a dual-porosity ePTFE implant introduced to address the shrinkage and migration seen with earlier types.[4][6]

Published surgeon series include a review of 175 SoftForm pieces placed in 69 patients and 106 Advanta implants in 42 patients,[4] and a satisfaction survey of patients who received SoftForm in the perioral region.[5] Surgeons who use ePTFE implants describe them as a permanent option for people who have been satisfied with injectable fillers.[6][7]

angle.text: The implant sits inside the lip and permanently adds volume or shape, so people choose it for fuller, more defined lips without periodic filler injections. It is a solid device rather than an injectable gel.

paras: Lip implants made of Gore-Tex are delivered as strips or tubes and sold under names including SoftForm.[1] Wikipedia presents them among several lip augmentation options that also include fillers, fat transfer, donor tissue and surgical flaps.[1]

Facial plastic surgery literature groups SoftForm with implants used in the nasolabial fold, melomental fold and lips, and a 2002 paper describes a technique and a dedicated instrument for inserting dual-porosity ePTFE implants.[3][4][5]

Dual porosity is the main design change in the Advanta implant: a 100 micron core with a 40 micron outer coat, compared with the 30 micron pores of earlier ePTFE products such as Gore-Tex and SoftForm, which Dermatology Times reported tended to shrink and migrate.[6] The coat limits capsule formation while anchoring the implant, and the exposed core allows tissue ingrowth along its length.[6]

Facial plastic surgeon William Truswell, who patented an insertion instrument, reported placing more than 300 Advanta implants over five to six years, typically two or three in the upper lip and one or two in the lower, through small mucosal incisions closed with a single stitch.[6] Indianapolis surgeon Barry Eppley describes placing Advanta in the office under local anaesthesia and nerve blocks, threading it through incisions at the mouth corners, and favours a split-implant technique with a central incision to keep depth symmetrical and avoid a tight upper lip.[7]

Wikipedia traces lip augmentation from failed paraffin injections around 1900, to liquid silicone from the early 1960s (abandoned about 30 years later over health concerns), to injectable bovine collagen around 1980, with many more substances arriving in the late 1990s [1]. Solid ePTFE implants sit alongside these as a surgical, non-resorbing option, and the published SoftForm and Advanta series were collected in the late 1990s and early 2000s [4][5].

In the same overview, the options for adding lip volume include hyaluronic acid gels such as Restylane (usually lasting about six months) and Juvederm, fat transfer, calcium hydroxylapatite, donor tissue and permanent PMMA microsphere products, each with different durations and complication profiles [1]. Wikipedia notes that results depend heavily on the provider's skill, and describes overfilling or poor placement as producing the 'trout pout' look [1].

A 2002 paper in Archives of Facial Plastic Surgery reported on 175 pieces of SoftForm (Collagen Corporation) placed in 69 patients over three years, plus 106 Advanta implants (Atrium Medical) in 42 patients between 1997 and 2000.[4] The author reported significant problems with shrinkage and migration of low-porosity ePTFE implants and preliminarily described a dual-porosity implant as offering a lower incidence of these complications and as subjectively softer once in place.[4]

A 2003 retrospective telephone survey in the same journal followed 38 of 50 patients (76 percent) who had Softform implants to the melolabial fold, melomental fold, upper lip and lower lip, at a mean of 22.7 months after the procedure, to assess satisfaction.[5]

Truswell reported that patients and their partners said kissing was unaffected and that correctly placed implants caused no numbness or loss of lip function; he had seen two infections and advised against use in very thin lips.[6] Eppley reported using Advanta for years without infection or extrusion and no removals, saw occasional uneven depths that he attributed to technique, and does not use it as a primary augmentation but for patients with a history of successful filler treatment who want a permanent option; he notes injectable fillers last up to about 9 to 12 months.[7]

Wikipedia lists implant-specific complications of lip augmentation as movement of the implant and extrusion through the tissue, and more general ones including bleeding, uneven lips and lumpiness.[1] The 2002 series reported shrinkage and migration with low-porosity implants.[4]

General lip-augmentation complications listed by Wikipedia also include redness, swelling and itching (with swelling and bruising lasting up to a week), bleeding, uneven lips, and lumps; people with certain conditions such as clotting or healing problems, active cold sores or severe hypertension are generally advised against lip augmentation, and smoking complicates healing [1]. A related PTFE-implant risk the authors describe is shrinkage of low-porosity material, which is the problem the dual-porosity design was proposed to address [4].
Surgeon-listed risks include infection, extrusion, asymmetric implant depth, a tight upper lip with one-piece implants, and oversizing; bruising and swelling are common after placement.[6][7]

Lip augmentation is a widely publicised cosmetic procedure, and Wikipedia reports that tabloids and offbeat websites often mock overdone results while practitioners emphasise provider skill [1]. The field has moved over time from silicone and collagen toward hyaluronic acid, fat transfer and minimally invasive options, with fine-gauge needles and topical anesthetics now common [1]. ePTFE implants are one of the older permanent options and are discussed in the facial plastic surgery literature as soft-tissue implants rather than as consumer products [3][4][5].

Two surgeon-reported studies examined SoftForm and related ePTFE implants in the perioral region: a case review of 175 SoftForm and 106 Advanta implants that described shrinkage and migration with low-porosity designs, and a 50-patient retrospective satisfaction survey.[4][5] A 2000 historical review covers the development and techniques of SoftForm for facial rejuvenation.[3]

timeline.event: Start of a three-year series of Advanta ePTFE implant placements later reported in Archives of Facial Plastic Surgery.[4]
Facial Plastic Surgery publishes a historical review of SoftForm for facial rejuvenation.[3]
A paper reports shrinkage and migration with low-porosity ePTFE implants and describes a dual-porosity design.[4]
A patient-satisfaction survey of SoftForm perioral implants is published.[5]
Dermatology Times reports on dual-porosity Advanta implants and insertion technique.[6]
Surgeon Barry Eppley describes his Advanta split-implant technique.[7]

card.summary: A strip or tube of expanded PTFE placed in the lip by a surgeon for permanent volume and definition, without repeat injections.
card.aka: SoftForm, Advanta, UltraSoft, ePTFE lip implant
card.note: Implant movement, extrusion, shrinkage and migration are reported complications.

quick.overview:
Gore-Tex lip implants are thin strips or tubes of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) that a surgeon places in the lip to add permanent volume. Wikipedia lists SoftForm, Advanta and UltraSoft as commercial versions, in diameters of 1.6 mm or 4.8 mm.

ePTFE is a long-established surgical material in vascular and facial plastic surgery. Surgeon-reported series from 2002 and 2003 describe outcomes in the lip, and a dual-porosity version (Advanta) was developed after shrinkage and migration were seen with earlier types.
quick.risks: Wikipedia lists implant movement and extrusion (breaking through the tissue) among complications of lip implants, along with bleeding, asymmetry and lumpiness. Surgeons report bruising and swelling after placement, and the literature describes shrinkage and migration with older low-porosity implants. Unlike hyaluronic acid fillers, an implant is a physical device rather than an injectable.
quick.how: A surgeon threads the implant through small incisions at the corners of the mouth or in the lip, often under local anaesthetic, so that it sits inside the lip and permanently adds volume. Some surgeons place two or three strips in the upper lip and one or two in the lower, or use a split-implant technique to keep depth even.
